\chapter{Thinking, Reading, Writing}
\label{ch:la-mind-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{38}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I think, I read, I understand and I write in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and name the English words each verb built.}

The chapter closes on scrībō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō and cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[cōgitō, cōgitāre]{cōgitō — thinking as driving things together}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-cogito}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Sciō} is knowing a fact you already hold. This verb is the work you do before you hold it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōgitō — \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Cōgitō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I think},\textquotedblright{} in the sense of turning something over. The dictionary form is \textbf{cōgitāre}. Both \emph{o}-vowels are long and the \emph{g} is hard: \emph{KOH-ghee-TAH-reh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cōgitō} — I think
  \item \textbf{cōgitās} — you think, to one person
  \item \textbf{cōgitat} — he thinks, she thinks
  \item \textbf{cōgitāmus} — we think
  \item \textbf{cōgitātis} — you think, to several people
  \item \textbf{cōgitant} — they think
\end{itemize}

Latin's other everyday verb here is \textbf{putō}, \textquotedblleft{}I reckon, I suppose\textquotedblright{} — lighter, closer to English \textquotedblleft{}I guess.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Cōgitāre} is \emph{co-} (\textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{}) welded onto \emph{agitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep driving about\textquotedblright{} — itself the restless form of \emph{agere}, \textquotedblleft{}to drive, to do.\textquotedblright{} Thinking, to a Roman, is not stillness: it is driving your material together and keeping it in motion.

English took the verb whole in \textbf{cogitate} and \textbf{cogitation}, and took the most quoted sentence in philosophy with it: \emph{cōgitō ergō sum}, \textquotedblleft{}I think, therefore I am\textquotedblright{} — whose second word is the \textbf{sum} you already know.

The engine underneath, \emph{agere}, is one of Latin's great suppliers: \textbf{act}, \textbf{action}, \textbf{agent}, \textbf{agenda} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be driven forward\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{agile}, \textbf{agitate}, \textbf{exact}, and \textbf{navigate} (\emph{nāvis}, \textquotedblleft{}ship,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{agere}). The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*ag-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to drive,\textquotedblright{} which in Greek became \emph{ágō} and gave \textbf{pedagogue} (\textquotedblleft{}child-leader\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{demagogue}.

\emph{Putāre} is worth its own paragraph. It first meant \textquotedblleft{}to prune a tree,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}to settle an account,\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}to consider\textquotedblright{} — and English inherited all three stages: \textbf{amputate}, \textbf{compute} (and its worn-down form \textbf{count}), \textbf{dispute}, \textbf{deputy}, \textbf{impute}, and \textbf{reputation}.

One flag. English \textbf{think} is Germanic, from the root that also gives \textbf{thank} — a thought and a grateful thought. It is not related to \emph{cōgitō}. Nor is \textbf{cognition}, which belongs to \emph{nōscō}, the other knowing verb.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitō\textquotedblright{} — I think, hard g
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitās, cōgitat\textquotedblright{} — you think, he or she thinks
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cōgitāmus, cōgitātis, cōgitant\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — cogitate, agent, agenda, compute
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I think\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Cōgitō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They think\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Cōgitant}.) What two pieces is the verb built from? (\emph{\textbf{Co-}}, \textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{agitāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to keep driving about\textquotedblright{}.) Which philosopher's sentence carries it, and which chapter-37 verb closes that sentence? (\emph{\textbf{Cōgitō ergō sum}} — and \textbf{sum}.) Which English word began as \emph{putāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to prune\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Amputate} — and \textbf{compute}, and \textbf{count}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[legō, legere]{legō — reading is picking things up}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-lego}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Cōgitō} drives ideas together. The next verb gathers something more concrete — and it is the single richest word in this book.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: legō — \textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Legō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I read}.\textquotedblright{} Its older and wider sense is \textquotedblleft{}I gather, I pick out.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{legere}. Every \emph{g} is hard and every vowel here is short: \emph{LEH-goh}, \emph{LEH-geh-reh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{legō} — I read
  \item \textbf{legis} — you read, to one person
  \item \textbf{legit} — he reads, she reads
  \item \textbf{legimus} — we read
  \item \textbf{legitis} — you read, to several people
  \item \textbf{legunt} — they read
\end{itemize}

Reading is the younger meaning, and you can feel how it arrived: you pick the letters up, one after another. A Roman normally did this aloud.

\begin{cousinweb}
The Proto-Indo-European root is \emph{\textbf{*leg-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to gather, to collect.\textquotedblright{}

Straight from \emph{legere} English has \textbf{legible}, \textbf{legend} (\textquotedblleft{}things to be read\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{lectern}, \textbf{lecture}, and — through Old French \emph{leçon}, from \emph{lectiōnem}, \textquotedblleft{}a reading\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{lesson}. A Roman \textbf{legion} was a \emph{legiō}, a levy of men picked out for service.

Prefixed, the verb becomes a machine. \emph{Con-} gives \textbf{collect} (gather together); \emph{sē-} gives \textbf{select} (gather apart); \emph{ē-} gives \textbf{elect} (pick out). \textbf{Neglect} is \emph{nec legere}, \textquotedblleft{}not to pick up.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Elegant} is \emph{ēlegāns} — originally an insult, \textquotedblleft{}too choosy.\textquotedblright{}

Greek inherited the same root as \emph{légō}, \textquotedblleft{}I gather, I speak,\textquotedblright{} and its noun \emph{lógos}, \textquotedblleft{}word, reason.\textquotedblright{} From those come \textbf{logic}, \textbf{catalogue}, \textbf{dialogue}, \textbf{analogy}, \textbf{anthology} (a flower-gathering), and the \emph{-logy} ending on every science you can name.

One caution. Latin \emph{lēx}, \emph{lēgis} (\textquotedblleft{}law\textquotedblright{}) — behind \textbf{legal}, \textbf{legislate}, \textbf{loyal}, and \textbf{privilege} — is often derived from \emph{legere}, \textquotedblleft{}what is read out.\textquotedblright{} That link is \textbf{debated}; treat it as a maybe.

And a false friend: English \textbf{read} is Germanic, from a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}to advise,\textquotedblright{} still visible in \textbf{riddle}. It has nothing to do with \emph{legō}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legō\textquotedblright{} — I read, hard g
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legis, legit\textquotedblright{} — you read, he or she reads
  \item \textquotedblleft{}legimus, legitis, legunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the English relatives — legible, collect, select, elegant
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Legō}.) \textquotedblleft{}They read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Legunt}.) What did the verb mean before it meant \textquotedblleft{}read\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To gather, to pick out}.) What does \textbf{neglect} literally say? (\emph{\textbf{Nec legere}}, \textquotedblleft{}not to pick up\textquotedblright{}.) Is English \emph{read} a relative? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic, from a word meaning \textquotedblleft{}to advise\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[intellegō, intellegere]{intellegō — reading between}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-intellego}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Legō} picks things out. Put one small word in front of it and you get the verb behind \textbf{intelligence} itself.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: intellegō — \textquotedblleft{}I understand\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Intellegō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I understand}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{intellegere}. It is \emph{legō} with a prefix, so the endings are the ones you have just learned: \emph{in-TEL-leh-goh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{intellegō} — I understand
  \item \textbf{intellegis} — you understand, to one person
  \item \textbf{intellegit} — he understands, she understands
  \item \textbf{intellegimus} — we understand
  \item \textbf{intellegitis} — you understand, to several people
  \item \textbf{intellegunt} — they understand
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Nōn intellegō} — \textquotedblleft{}I do not understand\textquotedblright{} — is the single most useful sentence in this chapter.

\begin{cousinweb}
The prefix is \emph{inter}, \textquotedblleft{}between, among.\textquotedblright{} Before an \emph{l} it wore down to \emph{intel-}. So \emph{intellegere} is \textbf{to pick out from among}, to read between one thing and another. Latin says outright what English only implies: understanding is discrimination.

The family in English is one of the most familiar in the language: \textbf{intellect}, \textbf{intellectual}, \textbf{intelligent}, \textbf{intelligence}, \textbf{intelligible} and \textbf{unintelligible}, and — borrowed back through Russian — \textbf{intelligentsia}. Military and diplomatic \textbf{intelligence} is the older sense of the noun: information gathered.

There is a spelling puzzle here worth solving. Classical Latin wrote \textbf{intellegō} with an \emph{e}, keeping the vowel of \emph{legō}; later Latin respelled it \emph{intelligō}. English took both, at different dates, which is why \textbf{intellect} keeps the \emph{e} while \textbf{intelligent} carries the \emph{i}. Two spellings, one verb.

\emph{Inter} on its own gave English \textbf{interval}, \textbf{interior}, \textbf{interrupt}, \textbf{international}, and \textbf{interest} — that last one already met as \emph{inter est}, \textquotedblleft{}it is between.\textquotedblright{}

Two flags. Latin had a second word for understanding, \emph{comprehendere}, \textquotedblleft{}to grasp together,\textquotedblright{} which gives \textbf{comprehend} and \textbf{comprehensive}; it is a different image and a different root. And English \textbf{understand} is Germanic, a compound of \emph{under} and \emph{stand} — no connection at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}intellegō\textquotedblright{} — I understand
  \item \textquotedblleft{}intellegis, intellegit\textquotedblright{} — you understand, he or she understands
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nōn intellegō\textquotedblright{} — I do not understand
  \item the English relatives — intellect, intelligent, intelligible
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I understand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Intellegō}.) \textquotedblleft{}I do not understand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Nōn intellegō}.) What two pieces is it built from? (\emph{\textbf{Inter}}, \textquotedblleft{}between,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{legere}, \textquotedblleft{}to pick out\textquotedblright{}.) Why does English have both \emph{intellect} and \emph{intelligent}? (\textbf{Two Latin spellings} — classical \emph{intellegō}, later \emph{intelligō}.) Is English \emph{understand} related? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[scrībō, scrībere]{scrībō — writing began as scratching, and the four together}

\label{lesson:LA-C38-scribo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Cōgitō} turns things over, \textbf{legō} takes words off a surface, \textbf{intellegō} picks them apart. One verb is left: the one that put them there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scrībō — \textquotedblleft{}I write\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Scrībō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I write}.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{scrībere}. The \emph{sc} is a plain \emph{sk} and the \emph{ī} is long and held: \emph{SKREE-boh}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{scrībō} — I write
  \item \textbf{scrībis} — you write, to one person
  \item \textbf{scrībit} — he writes, she writes
  \item \textbf{scrībimus} — we write
  \item \textbf{scrībitis} — you write, to several people
  \item \textbf{scrībunt} — they write
\end{itemize}

Note that the endings match \emph{legō} exactly. Two verbs, one pattern.

\begin{cousinweb}
The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*skreyb\textsuperscript{h}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to cut, to scratch, to incise.\textquotedblright{} That is not a metaphor. A Roman writing a note pressed a pointed stylus into a wax-coated board; writing \emph{was} scratching, and the verb never forgot it.

The English family is enormous and almost entirely transparent. Bare: \textbf{scribe}, \textbf{scribble}, \textbf{script}, \textbf{scripture}, \textbf{scrivener}. Compounded with a noun: \textbf{manuscript}, \textquotedblleft{}written by hand,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{manus}, the hand. Prefixed with a preposition, the verb runs the whole set — \textbf{describe} (write down), \textbf{prescribe} (write in advance), \textbf{subscribe} (write underneath, which is what signing a document was), \textbf{transcribe} (write across), \textbf{inscribe} (write into), \textbf{circumscribe} (write around), \textbf{proscribe} (post a name publicly, which in Rome meant a death sentence), \textbf{ascribe}, \textbf{conscript}, and \textbf{postscript}.

One quiet survivor: Old English borrowed \emph{scrībere} as \emph{scrīfan}, \textquotedblleft{}to impose a penance in writing,\textquotedblright{} and that gives \textbf{shrive}, \textbf{shrift}, and the Tuesday before Lent, \textbf{Shrove} Tuesday. When somebody gets \textbf{short shrift}, they are being given very little confession time.

Now the honest part. English \textbf{write} is \textbf{not} from this verb. It is Germanic, from a word that also meant \textquotedblleft{}to scratch, to tear\textquotedblright{} — two languages reaching the same image with two different words. \textbf{Scrape} and \textbf{scrub} are likewise Germanic and unrelated, however much they sound the part.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}scrībō, scrībis, scrībit\textquotedblright{} — I write, you write, he or she writes
  \item this chapter's four \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms — cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō
  \item the four \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms — cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit
  \item the English relatives — scribe, script, describe, manuscript
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give this chapter's four \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Cōgitō, legō, intellegō, scrībō}.) Now the four \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Cōgitat, legit, intellegit, scrībit}.) What did \emph{scrībere}'s root originally mean? (\textbf{To scratch, to incise} — a stylus in wax.) What does \textbf{subscribe} literally say? (\textbf{Write underneath} — to sign.) Is English \emph{write} from this verb? (\textbf{No} — it is Germanic, and happens to mean \textquotedblleft{}scratch\textquotedblright{} too.)
\end{tcolorbox}
